name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38
evidenceNote: The collagen-boosting claims rest on the supplier's lab and skin-sample tests. The only peer-reviewed human study is an industry-funded, open-label trial of 35 women using a serum that also contained vitamins C and E, so the peptide's own effect cannot be separated out.
summary: A three-amino-acid peptide with a fatty tail, used in anti-wrinkle creams at a few parts per million. Lab data are promising; human evidence is thin.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a short peptide of lysine, oxidized methionine, and lysine, linked to a fatty acid so it can enter the outer skin. Developed by the French ingredient maker Sederma, it is added to anti-aging serums and creams. Lab and skin-explant studies report that it signals skin cells to make more collagen and other support proteins. In people, the only published study tested it inside a vitamin C and E serum without a control group. As a cosmetic ingredient it needs no FDA approval.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is the ingredient-list name for palmitoyl-lysyl-dioxymethionyl-lysine, a chain of three amino acids attached to palmitic acid, a common fatty acid [1]. The middle amino acid is methionine in an oxidized form, which is why the code is sometimes written as KMO2K [1][2].

It comes from a family of lysine-based peptides patented by the French cosmetic ingredient company Sederma, with a priority date in 2009 [2]. The patent describes it as active at very low levels, on the order of a few parts per million in a finished product [2]. The published human study used it at 5 ppm, or five milligrams per kilogram of serum [1].

The fatty acid tail has a practical purpose. Attaching a palmitoyl group is a common way to help cosmetic peptides pass through the outer layer of skin and hold up against the skin's protein-cutting enzymes [3].

Cosmetic chemists group skin peptides into three types: signal peptides, carrier peptides, and peptides that interfere with nerve signals to muscle [3]. Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a signal peptide. The idea is that when the skin's supporting matrix breaks down, small protein fragments called matrikines tell nearby cells to repair it, and a synthetic mimic can send the same message [1][3].

In cell culture and in samples of donated human skin kept alive in the lab, the peptide has been reported to increase production of six matrix components: collagen types I, III, and IV, hyaluronic acid, fibronectin, and laminin [1][2]. Collagen gives skin much of its strength and hyaluronic acid helps it hold water. The patent also describes increased aquaporins, channels that move water through cells [2].

These results come from the supplier's own testing, filed as a patent rather than published in a peer-reviewed journal [1][2]. They show what the molecule can do to cells in a dish or a tissue sample. They do not show how much of a cream's peptide reaches the living cells of the dermis in real use.

No, and it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetics and their ingredients, apart from color additives, can be sold without FDA approval [4]. Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, so no regulator has reviewed evidence that it reduces wrinkles.

Whether a product counts as a cosmetic or a drug depends on what it claims. A product meant to change the structure or function of the body meets the legal definition of a drug, and the FDA judges intended use from labels, advertising, and websites [4]. That is why anti-aging products usually promise to improve the look of wrinkles rather than to rebuild collagen, even when the ingredient was chosen for its effect on collagen in the lab.

The only peer-reviewed human study found tested a serum that combined 15% vitamin C, vitamin E, and 5 ppm palmitoyl tripeptide-38 [1]. Thirty-five women with an average age of 64 and visible sun damage applied it to the face once a day for eight weeks, and researchers measured skin texture with 3D imaging and tone with photographs [1].

rows: Improved, in line with the instrument readings [1]

blocks.text: Several limits apply. There was no placebo or untreated comparison group, which the authors acknowledged [1]. The serum held three active ingredients, and vitamin C on its own is known to affect skin tone, so the study cannot say what the peptide contributed [1]. The trial was funded by the company that makes the serum, and the lead author works for a cosmetic science consultancy [1].

The study's authors also cite a vehicle-controlled trial of the peptide alone that reported smoother forehead and crow's feet lines at 5 ppm, but that trial appeared in a trade magazine rather than a peer-reviewed journal [1]. Until a controlled, independently run trial is published, the effect of the peptide by itself on wrinkles in people remains unproven.

sections.heading: Is it safe on the skin?

blocks.text: In the eight-week study, participants kept a daily log of side effects, and no adverse effects were attributed to the serum [1]. Thirty-five people over two months is far too few to detect uncommon reactions such as contact allergy.

The amounts used are tiny, a few parts per million, which limits exposure [1][2]. As with any cosmetic, irritation is more likely to come from the rest of the formula, such as high-strength vitamin C or fragrance, than from a trace peptide. There are no data on use during pregnancy or on broken skin.
